This is our kickoff for the outbreak management functional requirements, and it's the only session we have planned, so let's try to cover as much as we can."},{"id":"M1:T2","text":"Sure, some background first. Outbreak Management, or OM, is the PHIN functional area that's meant to support investigation, monitoring, management, analysis and reporting of a health event, or an act of bioterrorism. The core of any system supporting OM is being able to collect data on cases and exposures, and to create traceable links between all the appropriate entities. Because if you can trace how it's being transmitted and find the source of the health event, the response staff can contain it a lot more effectively."},{"id":"M1:T3","text":"Great, thanks. So let's start with the outbreak management functional requirements themselves. What are the main areas you need covered?"},{"id":"M1:T4","text":"Two big ones for me. First, analysis, visualization and report generation. Investigators should be able to produce both aggregated reports and individual reports about the affected entities and events. Second, system integration and data exchange. OM information has to be exchangeable, based on established standards, between the systems involved in investigating, identifying, confirming and reporting a health event."},{"id":"M1:T5","text":"Okay, got it."},{"id":"M1:T6","text":"And from my side, security and availability. Securing OM data means protecting it from corruption and from access by unauthorized people, but also protecting the actual systems supporting OM from sabotage or any other failure. And we need a plan in place for keeping things going when those systems aren't available."},{"id":"M1:T7","text":"Makes sense."},{"id":"M1:T8","text":"Let's move on to system architecture. What do you need there?"},{"id":"M1:T9","text":"One thing is structured data entry. The systems need to support structured entry for the common forms and fields, so we get data integrity, validity and standardization."},{"id":"M1:T10","text":"For us out in the field, computers running in disconnected mode should be able to reconnect to a server and share OM data with the other computers that are also working disconnected."},{"id":"M1:T11","text":"And the OM data should be synchronized, so every instance of the OM application working off the same server can share and use the same data."},{"id":"M1:T12","text":"Right."},{"id":"M1:T13","text":"Also, the systems should be able to electronically record and store data from remote devices, and that data might get uploaded to an aggregating system."},{"id":"M1:T14","text":"Okay."},{"id":"M1:T15","text":"Oh, and they should be able to use vocabulary that's domain-specific and configurable."},{"id":"M1:T16","text":"Good. Next topic, entity data. What do you need to capture about the entities involved?"},{"id":"M1:T17","text":"For persons involved in an investigation, we must capture demographic data: Subject ID, name, address, date of birth, gender, phone number, race, ethnicity and country of citizenship. And for organizations involved, say a local health department, a university, a professional association, we need the organization name, location and contact information."},{"id":"M1:T18","text":"So for organizations, things like a local health department, a university or a professional association, you'd capture name, location and contact info, right?"},{"id":"M1:T19","text":"Yes, exactly."},{"id":"M1:T20","text":"And animals too. For any animal involved in an investigation we must capture the type, like dog, monkey and so on, plus age, gender, the owner's name and address, color, weight and species."}]}
